claims.text: A uniform distribution of low-density elements induces beneficial lattice distortions in lightweight high-entropy alloys.
The lattice distortions produced by well-distributed light elements strengthen the alloy matrix by impeding dislocation motion.
Uniformly distributed low-density elements promote the formation of stable, coherent oxide layers such as Al2O3 or TiO2.
Protective oxide phases form in situ at high temperatures.
Stable, coherent oxide scales confer corrosion resistance.
Stable, coherent oxide scales confer high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The initial alloy can be synthesized with a homogeneous microstructure and uniformly distributed low-density elements.
A processing modification can induce elemental segregation in an otherwise compositionally identical alloy.
Heat treatment and cooling conditions can maintain a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Excessive thermal gradients can promote segregation or phase separation of light elements.
Relative to the same composition processed to allow segregation, the uniformly processed alloy will have higher yield strength.
Relative to the same composition processed to allow segregation, the uniformly processed alloy will have higher microhardness.
Relative to the same composition processed to allow segregation, the uniformly processed alloy will have better corrosion resistance.
Relative to the same composition processed to allow segregation, the uniformly processed alloy will have better high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Significant elemental segregation or phase separation will disable the proposed strengthening and environmental-resistance mechanism.
The magnitude of property improvements depends on the particular alloy system and processing parameters.
Failure of the segregation-induced specimen to show statistically significant reductions in strength, hardness, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance would falsify the hypothesis.
